newsitem.title: UK: Loyalists urged to hold truce, IRA slammed by Dublin.
newsitem.headline: Loyalists urged to hold truce, IRA slammed by Dublin.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister John Bruton accused the IRA of on Wednesday of a "cynical betrayal" of peace hopes by bombing Northern Ireland and likened their demand for unconditional peace talks to Nazi tactics.

Bruton said the attack on Britain's Lisburn army base on Monday had completed a "terrible triangle" of IRA violence this year after bombings in London and Manchester and the murder of an Irish policeman in the southern Irish town of Adare.
"The Lisburn bombing is a cynical betrayal by the IRA of the peace process. The IRA have now completed a terrible triangle," Bruton told the Irish parliament in Dublin.
"Those are the classic tactics of the National Socialists and Fascists during the 1920s and 1930s," he said.

The IRA admitted responsibility for the Lisburn bombing on Tuesday with a statement calling on Britain to allow its Sinn Fein political wing to take part in Belfast peace talks without the precondition of disarming or calling a new ceasefire.
It was the first IRA attack in Northern Ireland for more than two years and raised fears of revenge violence by Protestant Loyalist guerrilla groups which have stuck by a two-year truce until now.

Politicians appealed to Loyalist guerrillas not to retaliate for the Irish Republican Army bombing with anti-Catholic violence which would return Northern Ireland to the darkest days of its 25-year political and sectarian "Troubles."
Politicians representing the Protestant majority said the IRA had set a trap for Loyalists with their Lisburn bomb.

"As always, we will be doing everything in our power...to see that the Loyalist ceasefire stays intact," said David Adams, a leader of the Ulster Democratic Party (UDP), the political wing of the banned Ulster Defence Association (UDA).
"We have to realise that Loyalists up until now have refused to be drawn back in. Let's hope they realise yet again that that is what (IRA) republicans want and that they refuse to do it."

The Loyalists' political spokesmen are taking part in Belfast peace talks by virtue of the ceasefire by their guerrilla allies while Sinn Fein is banned because of the return to violence in February after a 17-month truce of the IRA.
In Washington a statement from the White House condemned the IRA action that injured 31 people, as "a barbaric act".
Anthony Lake, President Clinton's national security adviser, said that if Loyalists rejoined the conflict "it could destroy the future of Northern Ireland".
British Prime Minister John Major also appealed for calm following the IRA attack. The IRA seeks to oust Britain from Northern Ireland and unite the divided island.
"The Provisional IRA are trying to provoke a general return to violence in Northern Ireland. We must not let them succeed. I appeal to all Loyalists not to fall into this trap," Major said.
Media reports said that outlawed groups in the Loyalist umbrella organisation that led an onslaught on the Irish nationalist Catholic minority for 25 years met indvidually on Tuesday.
They said the Combined Loyalist Military Command (CLMC) would meet shortly to consider strategy after the IRA's admission of responsibility on Tuesday for the Lisburn bomb.

"We should avoid as best we can the cycle of violence that undoubtedly would take us to hell and back again," David Ervine of the Progressive Unionist Party (PUP), the political wing of the banned Ulster Volunteer Force, told Reuters.
